children: WSW, NY, September 8th, 2026, FinanceWire

A quiet but urgent audit is under way across the American defense industry. Prime contractors are combing through their most advanced hardware, part by part, in search of a component most people never think about: small, extremely powerful magnets. They sit inside fighter jets, guided missiles, drones, radar systems, and submarines, turning electricity into the precise motion that makes the hardware work. What the audits keep finding is the same uncomfortable answer: almost all of those magnets, or the raw materials inside them, come from China. A new federal rule is about to turn that into a serious problem for American defense companies, and a small U.S. producer called Evolution Metals & Technologies Corp. (Nasdaq: EMAT) is one of the few positioned to help solve it.

The rule is simple to state and hard to comply with. Starting January 1, 2027, U.S. defense contractors will be barred from using these magnets if the material inside them was mined or processed in China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea. There are a few narrow exceptions, but the window is closing fast. A July 2026 executive order made it much harder to get a waiver and pushed contractors to start proving exactly where every part in their supply chain comes from, all the way back to the mine.

That proof is hard to produce. The magnets are easy to miss, tucked inside parts like flight-control actuators, pumps, and missile guidance fins, and contractors are tracing them down through several tiers of suppliers, documenting where the metal in each one was mined and refined. The stakes make the work urgent: a single non-compliant magnet can hold up sign-off on an entire system, and once the deadline hits it can mean a lost contract or a program that no longer qualifies. The trouble is what these audits keep turning up: suppliers who can prove otherwise barely exist. China dominates nearly every step of this business: it mines most of the world's raw material, does the vast majority of the processing, and makes the overwhelming majority of the finished magnets. Building an alternative is slow and costly, and the hardest part is not digging material out of the ground. It is the middle steps, the processing and manufacturing that turn raw ore into a finished magnet, which can take years to set up.

That is exactly the gap Evolution Metals is built to fill. The company already makes these magnets outside of China, and its factories have been producing them commercially for more than 18 years. This year it hit a run of milestones that matter for the 2027 deadline. It passed the strict quality tests that major manufacturers require, across six different versions of its magnets. And it locked in its first supply of the key raw metal from outside China, sourced through partners in Vietnam and Japan, so it can document a clean, China-free trail from the mine to the finished product.

Now it is working on scale. Evolution Metals has placed firm orders for new production equipment due to arrive in late 2026, and is aiming for the capacity to make roughly 10,000 tons of magnets a year once that equipment is installed and running. That is a target, not current output, but it points the company straight at the demand the deadline is about to create, not only from weapons makers but from the broader shift to electric vehicles and clean energy, which rely on the same magnets.

Very few companies can prove their magnets are free of Chinese material today, and the pressure on the defense industry only grows as the deadline nears. A producer that already makes them, with the supply chain and the quality approvals in hand, is in a very different position than one still scrambling to catch up.
